lesson.title: The -ico & -al Bridges
lesson.subtitle: Adjectives in -ico with mandatory tildes, and invariable -al cognates

hook.title: Two Instant Adjective Bridges
hook.content: Welcome to Phase 2! Just as -ción and -dad handed you thousands of nouns, two suffixes hand you hundreds of descriptive adjectives on sight: English -ic / -ical becomes Spanish -ico / -ica (mágico, público, básico, económico, clásico, fantástico), and English -al stays spelled -al (natural, central, formal, personal, internacional, cultural)!

pattern.title: The Esdrújula Accent on -ico vs Final Stress on -al
pattern.content: Every single -ico/-ica word in Spanish carries a written accent mark on the vowel RIGHT BEFORE -ico: MÁ-gi-co, PÚ-bli-co, BÁ-si-co, fan-TÁS-ti-co! Meanwhile, every -al word stresses the final syllable (na-tu-RAL, cen-TRAL) and NEVER changes for masculine vs feminine in the singular: el hotel central, la casa central!
pattern.linguist_note: Words stressed on the third-from-last syllable (esdrújulas) always carry a written accent mark in Spanish orthography.
pattern.trap_note: Never add an *-a to -al adjectives for feminine nouns (*una idea naturala is impossible). Say una idea natural!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: mágico, público, básico, fantástico, natural, central
exercises.meaning: magical, public, basic, fantastic, natural (invariable), central (invariable)

exercises.prompt: Convert 'fantastic' into Spanish by snapping the accented stem and -ico together:
exercises.explanation: fantástico carries an esdrújula accent on the third syllable from the end.

exercises.prompt: Convert English 'classic / classical' into its masculine Spanish adjective (remember the accent!):
exercises.explanation: classic → clásico (single s, accent on á).

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The hotel is central and fantastic'
exercises.target_answer: El hotel es central y fantástico
exercises.meaning: The hotel is central and fantastic
exercises.explanation: El hotel es central (invariable -al) y fantástico (masculine -ico).

exercises.idea: say that it is a personal opinion
exercises.explanation: Es una opinión personal — personal follows opinión and needs no -a ending because it ends in -l!

diagnosis.cue: Place descriptive adjectives after the noun in Spanish: una opinión personal.

summary.outcome: Convert -ic/-ical adjectives to accented -ico/-ica and use -al adjectives as gender-invariable descriptors.

use_example.german: Es un hotel central y fantástico.
use_example.english: It is a central and fantastic hotel.

summary.takeaway: Every -ico/-ica word wears a written tilde; every -al word is gender-invariable in the singular.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([801] The Esdrújula Accent Gym): train your voice and eye on the rhythmic antepenultimate stress of -ico words.

foreshadow.line: Now that you can describe formal and personal situations, Topic 9 shows how Spanish encodes formal vs personal right into 'you' (tú vs usted).

payoff.text: The accent mark rule you saw on question words in Topic 7 now guides your voice on every -ico adjective.

mágico.etymology_derivation: Greek magikos → Latin magicus → mágico. All words in -ico carry an antepenultimate accent.

económico.etymology_derivation: Always accented on the third-from-last syllable.

natural.etymology_derivation: Latin nātūrālis. Words in -al have identical singular spelling in English and Spanish.

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.
